The Seelie are allies of spring and growth, while the Unseelie are those of cold and trickery. Each round, cards are dealt, where one player will split the possible actions between two piles, while the other will select who gets which set. You will each place, move, and remove influence across six regions and see who rules these sacred places, seeking majority control. The player who scores the best after three and six rounds will be declared the new ruler of this great isle. Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Overview This is an area majority game taking place across 6 rounds, scoring occurs in rounds 3 and 6 Turn First, each player MAY pick a Court card to play, which is kept secret for now Second, 4 Pact cards are revealed along with 1 Special Pact Third, 1st player splits these cards along with the 2nd player token however they wish into 2 piles Fourth, 2nd player picks a pile with 1st player getting the unselected pile Fifth, starting with 1st player each player plays all their gained cards in an order of their choosing, any unused cards are simply discarded. If a Court card was chosen earlier, this can be played at any point like a Pact card. Once player 2 has played all their cards which they wish, the round ends Scoring On the 3rd round, score each region based on whoever has the most influence tiles there. Ties mean no one wins the region. After which, flip the scoring tiles to their light side ready for the 2nd half. At the end of the 6th round, do the same. Whoever scores the most at the end of the 6th round, wins! [Rating: 2/10] A strictly 2-player "area control" game is suspect out of the gate. Yes, you'll be placing and moving cubes into various areas worth variable numbers of points but given the obvious back-and-forth turn structure, this gives less of an impression of "area control" and more of a somewhat standard tug-of-war. The incorporation of an "I cut, you choose" mechanism is neat and feels novel at first, but the variety of cards therein is notably slender. I have not played enough games to say for sure, but I could imagine things becoming very homogenous after dozens of plays. A respectable little time-ki

[Rating: 4/10] A split 'n choose carousel that has me green around the gills, since I'm naturally biased against area control.  Its saving grace: High-speed games can be knocked out in 15-20 minutes. Which for me puts it into the category of indigestible filler.

[Rating: 4/10] I heard a lot about this game and was eager to try it on BGA. It's a two-player I-cut-you-choose game of tense decisions and double-thinking. Maybe. I found it to be a tedious game of "I put one here" "Now I put one there" "Now I put one there" "Now I put one there" and so on, a prolonged slap-fight that outstays its welcome. There must be more here, given others' reactions to it, but I sure didn't see it.

[Rating: 5/10] Extremely pretty, and a fun play pattern. Hasn't been a good fit, gameplay-wise, with the people I've played with so far. I've played four games with three different people, and every single matchup felt like one of the factions had a very strong advantage over the other.  I'm going to gift it to a couple who I think will like the vibe and hopefully have more success with the gameplay.  Sold in the 2026 annual swap meet.

[Rating: 5/10] Based on 1 play:  Not sure if it's just the factions we played with or what, but it just seemed too easy to decide how to divide the cards in this so the whole thing felt pretty flat. I love I Split, You Choose as a mechanic because usually it leads to tense choices, but here it just felt lifeless.  Doesn't help that Marabunta exists as a direct comparison - another ISYC area control 1v1 game where each split feels absolutely AGONIZING. This is just missing some of that mathematical magic I don't understand but is critical to making a game like this feel dynamic and dramatic.  Curious to give 

[Rating: 5/10] Interesting area control with an "I cut you choose" mechanism. It's simple majority area control with draftable abilities and asymmetric player powers. A bunch of plays would probably tease out the different strategies and make the game shine. A single play didn't do much for me.

[Rating: 6/10] Bare bones two-player area control cube shifter. It's fine! The production is excellent.

[Rating: 6/10] While I split you choose games are not my favorite, I was very excited about the mythological factions in this game.  I think I had more fun just reading what each one did and enjoying the illustrations than I had playing the game.  But I highly recommend for others who enjoy 2 player, I split you choose style games!

[Rating: 6/10] First impression: nice! The factions do guarantee reasonable replayablity, but I fear the 'I split you choose' mechanism will get old fast otherwise. And going second in round 3 and 6 seems like a huge advantage unless you get very nerfed cards. Let's see how multiple plays hold up. Edit: yes, the excitement died fast.

[Rating: 6/10] I like the theme. Gameplay is conceptually interesting but I feel like is a little too directly zero sum rather than having some interesting maneuvering. It seems the decisions is almost all parsing out the I split you choose, and once you've parsed that out you've already basically decided where you would place/move pieces around or respond to your opponent.
